concepts.title: Surface vs Bulk
concepts.contentHtml:
Atoms at a surface have fewer neighbors than those in the bulk — bonds are unsatisfied or rearranged. This costs energy: surface energy γ (J/m²) is the work to create unit area of new surface.

Liquid water has γ ≈ 0.072 J/m² — high enough that drops form spheres (minimizing area for a given volume). Mercury's γ ≈ 0.5 J/m² — even more striking; it beads on glass.

For nanoparticles, surface atoms are a large fraction of the total. A 2-nm gold particle has ~50% of its atoms at the surface — its properties differ from bulk gold dramatically.

concepts.title: Wetting and Contact Angles
concepts.contentHtml:
Place a drop on a surface. The angle between the drop and the surface — the contact angle θ — measures wetting.

θ < 90°: hydrophilic. θ > 90°: hydrophobic. The lotus effect (θ > 150°) — superhydrophobic surfaces — combines low surface energy and microtexture so water rolls off, picking up dirt as it goes.

Young's equation balances the three interfacial tensions at the contact line: γ_sv = γ_sl + γ_lv cos θ.

concepts.title: Why Small Things Are Different
concepts.contentHtml:
Surface effects scale with area; bulk effects with volume. Halve the linear size, and surface fraction doubles. Nanoparticles are a regime where surface chemistry dominates.

Gold is inert in bulk but a powerful catalyst as 5-nm nanoparticles. Silver melts at 962 °C as bulk but at ~700 K as 4-nm clusters. Nanocrystals of semiconductors have tunable colors.

Designing materials means understanding both the bulk and the surface — and how they couple.

concepts.title: Physisorption vs Chemisorption
concepts.contentHtml:
Physisorption: weak van der Waals attraction. Energies of 5-50 kJ/mol. Reversible at modest temperatures. Doesn't change the molecule's structure.

Chemisorption: a chemical bond forms with the surface. Energies of 100-500 kJ/mol. The molecule's bonds may rearrange (e.g., H₂ dissociates on metals to give two H atoms each bound separately).

Chemisorption often precedes a catalytic reaction; physisorption can collect molecules on the surface from a gas phase.

concepts.title: Adsorption Isotherms
concepts.contentHtml:
The Langmuir isotherm models monolayer adsorption: θ = K·P / (1 + K·P), where θ is fraction of surface sites occupied.

The BET isotherm extends to multilayer adsorption — used to measure surface area of porous materials by N₂ adsorption at 77 K.

Knowing surface area is essential for catalysis. Activated carbon, zeolites, and MOFs achieve thousands of m²/g — comparable to a basketball court of surface in a sugar cube of material.

concepts.title: Surface Diffusion & Reactions
concepts.contentHtml:
Adsorbed species are not static. They diffuse along the surface, finding favorable sites or each other. Diffusion barriers on metals are typically 10-30% of the binding energy.

Surface reactions involve adsorption, surface diffusion, reaction at adjacent sites, and desorption of products. The rate-limiting step can be any of these.

Modern STM movies show single atoms diffusing across surfaces and reacting. Computational chemistry can map all the steps and barriers; together they give detailed mechanistic pictures.

title: Heterogeneous Catalysis
description: Most industrial chemistry happens at surfaces

concepts.title: The Haber-Bosch Process
concepts.contentHtml:
N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃ on iron catalyst at ~400 °C and 200 atm. The Haber-Bosch process produces ~150 million tonnes of ammonia per year — the basis of modern fertilizer and roughly half the nitrogen in food we eat.

Mechanism: H₂ dissociates on Fe; N₂ adsorbs and dissociates (rate-limiting); N atoms hydrogenate sequentially to NH₃.

It consumes 1-2% of global energy. Replacing it with renewable-electricity-driven nitrogen reduction is an active research goal.

concepts.title: Catalytic Converters
concepts.contentHtml:
The three-way catalytic converter in every modern car uses Pt, Pd, and Rh on a ceramic honeycomb. It converts CO → CO₂, unburned hydrocarbons → CO₂ + H₂O, and NOx → N₂.

The catalyst's huge effective surface area (~10⁴ m² in a small device) is what makes the conversion fast enough. Without catalytic converters, urban air would be much worse than it is.

concepts.title: Volcano Plots & Sabatier Principle
concepts.contentHtml:
Sabatier's principle: the best catalyst binds intermediates with intermediate strength. Too weak → no activation. Too strong → poisoning, slow desorption.

Plotting activity vs binding energy gives a volcano plot. Best catalysts sit at the peak. For ammonia synthesis, that's iron — not coincidentally what Haber found by trial.

Modern computational catalysis maps activity descriptors across many materials, accelerating discovery of catalysts with optimal binding.

concepts.title: Self-Assembled Monolayers
concepts.contentHtml:
Drop a thiol-functionalized molecule onto a gold surface and a single ordered layer assembles spontaneously — sulfur atoms anchor to gold, hydrocarbon chains pack via van der Waals.

Self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) let chemists tailor surface properties precisely. Hydrophobic, hydrophilic, charged, biologically active — design the molecule, get the surface.

SAMs are used in biosensors, microfluidics, organic electronics, and contact-printed patterns at the nanometer scale.

concepts.title: Lipid Membranes
concepts.contentHtml:
Phospholipids in water spontaneously form bilayers — hydrophobic tails sequestered inside, hydrophilic heads on both surfaces. Cell membranes are an evolved version of this same physics.

Adding curvature constraints, you get vesicles (lipid spheres) or tubular structures. The 2024 Nobel went to Schütz for entropic membrane biophysics.

Self-assembled lipid systems underlie cells, drug delivery liposomes, and the lipid nanoparticles that delivered mRNA COVID vaccines — billions of doses worth.

concepts.title: Block Copolymer Microphase Separation
concepts.contentHtml:
A block copolymer (poly-A linked to poly-B) microphase-separates into ordered nanostructures: lamellae, cylinders, spheres, or gyroids. Self-assembly is driven by entropy + enthalpy balances.

Used in nanolithography (templating below the optical diffraction limit), filtration membranes, and ion-conducting electrolytes.

Biological example: silk forms ordered β-sheet domains separated by amorphous regions — its tunable properties come from the block-copolymer-like structure.

concepts.title: Metal-Organic Frameworks (MOFs)
concepts.contentHtml:
MOFs are crystalline networks of metal nodes and organic linkers. Some have surface areas exceeding 7000 m²/g — a single gram having more surface than a football field.

Their tunable porosity makes them perfect for gas storage (hydrogen, methane, CO₂), separation, and catalysis. Hundreds of thousands of MOFs have been synthesized; databases predict properties of millions more.

Yaghi's pioneering work on MOFs since the 1990s has launched an entire subfield. Industrial applications (carbon capture, gas drying) are emerging.

concepts.title: Single-Atom Catalysis
concepts.contentHtml:
Heterogeneous catalysts traditionally use small metal nanoparticles. Single-atom catalysts disperse metal atoms one at a time on a support — every metal atom is a potential active site.

Maximum atom efficiency. Often unique selectivity because there are no metal-metal interactions. The downside: harder to synthesize and stabilize.

Pt single atoms on N-doped carbon, for example, are active for hydrogen evolution at remarkably low loadings — important for cost reduction in fuel cells and electrolysis.

concepts.title: Electro- and Photocatalysis
concepts.contentHtml:
Driving surface reactions with electricity (instead of heat or stoichiometric reagents) is the basis of fuel cells, electrolyzers, and the hoped-for renewable hydrogen economy.

Photocatalysis uses sunlight directly. TiO₂ and related semiconductors split water (in principle); newer materials and dyed structures push toward practical solar fuels.

Bridging chemistry, materials science, and electrochemistry, this is one of the most active areas in surface chemistry today.
